analysis.one_liner: Requires Medicare drug plans to reveal how pharmacies are paid and restrict pharmacy benefit managers' self-dealing.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in two House committees until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill targeted how Medicare prescription drug plans pay pharmacies and how pharmacy benefit managers treat patient data. It would require plans to update and disclose pharmacy reimbursement rates at least weekly, reveal the price sources they use, and set up appeals when a payment falls below what the pharmacy paid for the drug. It would also bar pharmacy benefit managers from steering patients to pharmacies they own without written patient consent, and from offering incentives limited to their own pharmacies.
analysis.who_benefits: Community and independent pharmacies gain the most: they would learn the price benchmarks used to reimburse them, get weekly updates tied to real acquisition costs, and gain an appeal process when reimbursements fall below what the pharmacy actually paid. Medicare enrollees gain privacy protections, since pharmacy benefit managers could not send their identifiable prescription data to PBM-owned pharmacies or pressure them to fill prescriptions at those pharmacies.

how_it_helps.text: Requires Medicare drug plans to update pharmacy reimbursement benchmarks at least every 7 days to reflect the market price of acquiring a drug.
Requires plan sponsors to disclose the sources used to set those price updates, and to reveal all individual drug prices in advance if the source is not publicly available.
Requires a process to appeal and resolve disputes when a reimbursement price is less than the pharmacy's acquisition cost for the drug.

Bars pharmacy benefit managers from transmitting personally identifiable claims data to a pharmacy they own unless the enrollee voluntarily opted in, in writing or by secure electronic means, to fill that prescription there.
Bars pharmacy benefit managers from requiring or incentivizing enrollees to use pharmacies in which the PBM has an ownership interest.

analysis.who_pays: Pharmacy benefit managers and the Medicare drug plan sponsors that contract with them bear the cost: they lose discretion over reimbursement formulas, must maintain weekly price updates, disclosures, and appeals processes, and forgo tools that steer patients toward their own pharmacies. Some cost may pass through to Medicare Part D premiums.
analysis.who_pays_short: Pharmacy benefit managers and drug plan sponsors

drawbacks.text: Reimbursement mandates on plan sponsors and pharmacy benefit managers could raise Medicare Part D administrative costs, and sponsors might pass those costs to enrollees through premiums.

Weekly reimbursement updates and advance disclosure of unpublished price lists could reduce plan sponsors' flexibility to negotiate drug costs, potentially raising Medicare's overall prescription drug spending.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The transparency and appeal provisions directly protect independent pharmacies from being reimbursed below their acquisition cost, and the data-privacy rules limit PBM self-dealing at patients' expense. The tradeoff is higher compliance costs for plan sponsors and PBMs, some of which could reach enrollees through premiums or reduced plan flexibility. On balance, the transparency benefits appear targeted and the compliance burden moderate, but the bill's design leaves open how much cost pass-through might occur.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to committees, then sent to a House Energy and Commerce subcommittee, and no further action was ever taken before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Doug Collins of Georgia introduced the bill on April 9, 2014, joined by Rep. Dave Loebsack as an original cosponsor.
The bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means Committees on April 9, 2014.
On April 11, 2014, it was referred to the Health Subcommittee within Energy and Commerce.
No further legislative action was recorded, and the bill expired when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmacy benefit managers and Medicare drug plan sponsors are better off: no reimbursement transparency or PBM self-dealing restrictions took effect, since the bill never advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: PBM and drug plan sponsor interests

industries.note: The bill would bar PBMs from transmitting identifiable claims data to pharmacies they own without patient opt-in, and from requiring or incentivizing enrollees to use PBM-owned pharmacies. It would also force their reimbursement practices into the open, including an appeals process when a plan pays a pharmacy less than the pharmacy paid for the drug.

industries.industry: Medicare Part D prescription drug plan sponsors
industries.note: Plan sponsors would face new contractual obligations: weekly reimbursement updates, disclosure of pricing sources, advance disclosure of unpublished prices, and a dispute-resolution process. These requirements raise compliance costs and constrain how sponsors set pharmacy payment rates.

Pharmacies would see reimbursement benchmarks updated at least weekly to reflect actual acquisition costs, would learn the sources used to set their payment rates, and could appeal reimbursements that fall below what the drug cost them to buy.
The bill would remove the enrollment-data advantage and steering incentives that let PBM-owned pharmacies capture prescriptions that patients might otherwise fill elsewhere.
